title: Invert, Always Invert: Plan a Family Gathering by Asking How to Ruin It
topic: tư duy: tư duy ngược và tiền-khám-nghiệm
unit: Chặng 1/12 · Ngôi nhà & gia đình Việt · Tuần 1/4: Gia đình, họ hàng & xưng hô
summary: Inversion means asking how you would fail and then avoiding those things. From Jacobi's maxim and Charlie Munger's 1986 'how to guarantee a life of misery' speech to Gary Klein's premortem, the tool turns this week's knowledge about kinship, anniversaries and in-laws into a concrete checklist, with its limits and three ways to practise.
body:
Suppose someone asks you: "How do you make a family gathering go well?" Most of us freeze, or produce something vague: be warm, be respectful, help out. Now try a different question: "How would you *guarantee* that the death-anniversary meal (*đám giỗ*) ends in a quarrel?" Suddenly the answers pour out. Arrive late. Call an elderly relative by the wrong kinship term (*xưng hô sai vai*). Ask your cousin, in front of everyone, why she still isn't married. Compare your aunt's cooking unfavourably with your mother's. Sit on your phone while the women carry trays.

That second question is a thinking tool called **inversion**. Instead of asking how to succeed, you ask how to fail, and then you avoid those things. It sounds like a trick. It is actually one of the most reliable ways to see a problem clearly.

## Where the idea comes from

The phrase most people associate with inversion is "Invert, always invert." It is attributed to the 19th-century German mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi, who found that many hard problems became easier when restated backwards.

The idea reached a wide audience through Charlie Munger, the long-time business partner of Warren Buffett. On June 13, 1986, Munger gave a graduation speech at the Harvard School in Los Angeles. Instead of telling the students how to be happy, he told them how to guarantee a life of misery. He began with three prescriptions he credited to the television host Johnny Carson: take mood-altering chemicals, be envious, and be resentful. Then he added four of his own: be unreliable; learn everything from your own experience rather than from the mistakes of others; go down and stay down when life knocks you over; and ignore the story of the rustic who said, "I wish I knew where I was going to die, and then I'd never go there."

The joke works because the advice is reversed. Read it backwards and you have a serious guide to a good life: be reliable, learn from others, get back up, and pay attention to where disasters happen so you can stay away.

## Why thinking backwards works

There are at least three reasons.

**Failure is more concrete than success.** "A good family gathering" is a fuzzy target. "Uncle Ba storms out because someone mentioned the land dispute" is a specific event. Our minds are better at generating specific, vivid scenarios than abstract ideals, so the inverted question produces more usable answers.

**Avoiding errors is often easier than achieving brilliance.** You may not know how to be the most charming daughter-in-law in the extended family. You certainly know how to avoid criticising your mother-in-law's cooking at the first anniversary meal. In many social situations, most of the value comes from not making a handful of predictable mistakes.

**It gets around optimism.** When we plan, we picture things going right. Inversion forces us to picture them going wrong, which is exactly the part our optimism hides.

## A close cousin: the premortem

The psychologist Gary Klein turned inversion into a team exercise he called the **premortem**, described in the *Harvard Business Review* in September 2007. A postmortem asks why a patient died. A premortem happens before the project starts: the leader tells the team, "Imagine it is a year from now and this project has failed badly. Write down every reason why." Everyone writes privately, then the reasons are read out one by one, and the plan is strengthened against them.

Klein's article cites a 1989 study by Deborah Mitchell, Jay Russo and Nancy Pennington, which found that imagining an event had *already* happened, a technique they called "prospective hindsight", increased people's ability to correctly identify reasons for future outcomes by 30%. Saying "it failed, why?" seems to unlock explanations that "could it fail?" does not.

## Applying it to the family this week

All week we have been looking at kinship terms, the paternal and maternal sides, anniversaries, and how to talk with elders and in-laws. Inversion is a way of turning all that knowledge into a checklist.

**Example 1: The first Tết as a new daughter-in-law.** Ask: how could I make sure my husband's family thinks badly of me by the third day? Possible answers:

- Arrive at the paternal home after the elders have already done the New Year's Eve offering.
- Spend the first morning at my own parents' house without discussing it with my husband first.
- Hand the red envelopes (*lì xì*) to the children in the wrong order of seniority.
- Correct my mother-in-law about how to arrange the five-fruit tray (*mâm ngũ quả*).
- Complain about my in-laws in a group chat my sister-in-law can read.

Now flip each line into an action: agree the schedule with your husband early; ask in advance about the order of visits and gifts; observe the house's customs before suggesting changes. Notice that none of this required you to know the "perfect" behaviour. You only needed to see the obvious traps.

**Example 2: Interviewing grandmother for the family tree.** How could I guarantee she never wants to talk about family history again? Rush her. Interrupt her stories to ask for dates. Correct her memory in front of others. Press on painful subjects such as relatives lost in the war. Post her personal details online without asking. The inverted list is, almost line by line, the method in today's article on drawing a family tree.

**Example 3: At the office.** The same tool works at work. Before a meeting where you will present a new procedure to the ward (*phường*) leadership, ask: how could this presentation fail? You use jargon the older officials don't share. You criticise the old procedure that the deputy chairman designed. You have no answer to "how much will it cost?" You run fifteen minutes over. Each failure points to a specific fix.

## Where inversion can mislead

Like any tool, inversion has limits.

- **Avoiding failure is not the same as achieving something.** A family gathering with no quarrels can still be cold and joyless. After you have cleared the traps, you still need the positive question: what would make this warm?
- **It can feed anxiety.** For someone who already worries a lot, listing every way things can go wrong may make them freeze. The point is to produce a short list of likely, avoidable failures, not an endless catalogue of disasters.
- **Your list reflects your blind spots.** If you have never lived in your husband's region, you may not know that a particular dish or word is offensive there. This is why the premortem works best with several people, and why asking a trusted insider ("what do people in your family usually get upset about?") is part of the method.

## How to practise

Inversion becomes useful only when it is a habit. Three small exercises:

1. **The two-minute flip.** Before any event that matters (a family meal, a difficult conversation, a meeting), write the sentence "This went badly because..." and finish it five times. Then pick the two most likely items and plan for them.
2. **Invert a piece of advice.** Take a proverb and reverse it to see what it is really warning against. "A word costs nothing, so choose your words to fit" (*Lời nói chẳng mất tiền mua, lựa lời mà nói cho vừa lòng nhau*) inverts to: the cheapest way to lose goodwill is careless speech. That tells you where to put your attention.
3. **Run a mini-premortem with someone else.** Before the next family event, ask your sibling or spouse: "Imagine it's over and it went badly. What happened?" You will be surprised how quickly they name something you had not thought of.

## In short

Inversion means approaching a goal from the other end: ask how you would fail, then avoid those things. Jacobi used it for mathematics, Munger for life choices, Klein for project teams. In a Vietnamese family full of unwritten rules, it is especially handy, because the ways to give offence are often clearer than the ways to please. Clear the traps first, then add warmth.

check.q: Why does asking 'how would this fail?' often produce more useful answers than 'how do I succeed?'
check.a: Failures are concrete and vivid while success is fuzzy, avoiding a few predictable mistakes delivers much of the value in social situations, and the question bypasses our natural optimism.

check.q: Name one limit of inversion and how to compensate for it.
check.a: Avoiding failure does not create warmth or success, so follow it with the positive question; or, since your list reflects blind spots, ask an insider or run the exercise with others.

try: Before your next family meal or important meeting this week, write 'This went badly because...' and finish it five times. Pick the two most likely items, do one thing to prevent each, and afterwards note whether either trap appeared.
